tips.title: Enable two-factor authentication on email, payment, and social accounts; prioritize phone pop-ups over SMS codes
tips.cost: No cost involved. Each account takes just two to three minutes to set up once.
tips.inPlainWords: Two-factor authentication means an extra verification step beyond the password when logging in. Using a pop-up prompt on your phone that requires a single tap to confirm blocks over 90% of phishing and account theft attempts. In contrast, older verification methods such as answering questions like “Where did you log in last time?” or “What is your backup email?” only block around 10% of such attacks.
tips.benefit: Google analyzed 350,000 real-world account hijacking attempts. For authentication methods relying on device verification — such as phone pop-ups or physical security keys — over 94% of phishing-related hijacking attempts and 100% of automated hijacking attempts were prevented. These automated attempts involve bots using leaked passwords to try logging into accounts in bulk. For verification based on answering personal questions, only 10% of phishing attempts and 73% of automated attempts were blocked.
tips.sources: Doerfler P, Thomas K, Marincenko M, et al. (2019). Evaluating Login Challenges as a Defense Against Account Takeover. The World Wide Web Conference (WWW '19). <https://doi.org/10.1145/3308558.3313481>
tips.caveats: The same study also found that these verification methods occasionally block legitimate users from accessing their accounts. 52% of real users failed to log in on their first try. However, 97% of them eventually gained access. It is recommended to enable this feature on email accounts first, as most other accounts allow password recovery via email.

tips.title: Use a unique password solely for your email
tips.cost: No cost involved. Storing it in a password manager eliminates the need to memorize it. The real challenge lies in breaking the old habit of reusing one password across multiple sites.
tips.inPlainWords: If a password you use elsewhere gets stolen, attackers can use it to log straight into your email account. Once they gain access to your email, they can reset passwords for any other accounts linked to it. Therefore, your email password must be unique and never reused anywhere else.
tips.benefit: Credential stuffing is one of the easiest attack methods: attackers simply test stolen passwords against other accounts. If your email password is compromised, all accounts that rely on it for password recovery become vulnerable too. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency recommends using a distinct, strong password of at least 16 characters for every account, and storing it via a password manager.
tips.caveats: If you struggle to memorize passwords, use the built-in password manager in your web browser. It stores passwords for each site for you, which is far safer than reusing the same password everywhere. Avoid saving passwords in WeChat favorites or note-taking apps.

tips.title: Set a screen lock on your phone and a PIN for the SIM card
tips.cost: No cost at all. You only need to set the screen lock and the SIM PIN once each.
tips.inPlainWords: The SIM card is that tiny card inside your phone that receives SMS verification codes. If your phone gets lost, a finder can remove the card and insert it into another phone to receive those codes, then reset all your accounts one by one. Setting a PIN on the SIM card means that whenever the card is moved to another phone, the user must enter that PIN before the phone can be used — effectively blocking that path.
tips.benefit: Without a SIM PIN, a finder can easily move your SIM card to another phone, receive verification codes, and reset all your accounts. With a PIN in place, that entire process is prevented, keeping your accounts safe even if your phone is lost.
tips.sources: author’s experience, no direct literature; Reserve Bank of India. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; CERT-In. <https://www.cert-in.org.in/>
tips.caveats: You can set the SIM PIN under “SIM card lock” in your phone settings. The default factory codes are usually 1234 or 0000. If you enter the wrong code three times in a row, you’ll need the PUK code provided by your carrier to unlock it. After setting the PIN, be sure to write it down somewhere safe.

tips.title: Follow these steps if you lose your phone: block the SIM card, remotely lock it, change passwords, file a police report, and freeze your bank cards if needed.
tips.cost: No cost involved. Completing all steps takes just a few minutes.
tips.inPlainWords: The order of actions matters more than speed. First, block the SIM card to cut off access to verification codes. Next, remotely lock the phone. Then, use a computer to change your email and payment passwords. After that, file a police report to obtain a receipt. Finally, freeze your bank cards as needed. Even if you’re using someone else’s phone, you can still call your carrier to block the SIM card.
tips.benefit: Following the correct sequence is more important than acting quickly. Step one is blocking the SIM card, which severs the main channel for verification codes. Step two involves remotely locking the phone and erasing all its contents. Step three requires changing your email and payment passwords from a computer. Step four is filing a police report to get a receipt. Finally, freeze your bank cards if necessary. The Federal Communications Commission also advises that even if you believe you merely misplaced your phone, you should still remotely lock it. If it’s stolen, file a police report immediately, providing the phone’s model and IMEI number, and inform your carrier right away.
tips.sources: US FCC. Protect Your Smart Device. <https://www.fcc.gov/consumers/guides/protect-your-mobile-device>; The sequence of steps is based on the author’s experience; see section 7 for a replacement ID card, and section 8 about credit information for fake loans.
tips.caveats: Also note the city where you registered your phone number, as customer service agents will ask for this information. You can still call carrier hotlines from someone else’s phone to block your SIM card.

tips.title: If your card is used fraudulently, report and freeze it first; your liability depends on how fast you report
tips.cost: No cost. Report on the bank's hotline and in writing, then on 1930.
tips.inPlainWords: The RBI's 2017 circular on unauthorised electronic transactions limits your liability if you report at once: zero liability where the fraud is due to a third party and you report within three working days. The bank must credit the amount within 10 working days. Report to the bank and on 1930, and keep the acknowledgement.
tips.benefit: The RBI circular sets a zero-liability rule for a third-party breach reported within three working days, and limited liability for a delay. The bank must resolve the complaint within 90 days. The IT Act and the BNS cover the fraud. A chargeback is separate from the bank's liability. A bank cannot make you pay for its own security failure.
tips.sources: Reserve Bank of India, customer protection circular on unauthorised electronic transactions. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. <https://cybercrime.gov.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: A delay can shift part of the liability to you. Do not share the OTP or PIN, even with a caller who claims to be from the bank. Keep the card blocked until the investigation ends.

tips.title: Periodically check the devices logged into your account and any authorized apps, then remove the ones you no longer use
tips.cost: No cost at all. It only takes a few minutes each time. The hard part is that there’s no reminder — you have to remember to do it yourself.
tips.inPlainWords: “Logged-in devices” refer to the phones and computers that can still access your account right now. Account thieves often lie low for a while before making their move. If you see any unfamiliar devices on the list, or third-party apps you no longer use still linked to your account, log out from all devices and change your password right away.
tips.benefit: Account theft rarely happens instantly — attackers usually spend some time lurking first. The list of logged-in devices shows all phones and computers currently able to access your account, while the list of authorized apps shows all third-party services you’ve given permission to log in using your account. Any unknown devices or unused third-party apps on these lists are the easiest clues to spot.
tips.sources: author’s experience, no direct literature; Reserve Bank of India. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; CERT-In. <https://www.cert-in.org.in/>
tips.caveats: This feature is available in WeChat, Alipay, email accounts, Apple ID, and Android accounts. If you spot any unfamiliar devices, simply log out from all devices and change your password.

tips.title: Don’t tap “Allow all” just to use an app: the data isn’t mandatory, and refusing to share it won’t block service access
tips.cost: No cost involved. The hard part is resisting the urge to tap “Allow all.”
tips.inPlainWords: Apps request your data. If that data isn’t strictly necessary to deliver the service, the app can’t deny you access just because you refuse to share it. It may only collect what it actually needs. For instance, a map app needs your location, but a flashlight app has no business asking for your contacts list.
tips.benefit: Two key legal points apply here. First, providers may not deny products or services on the grounds that a user hasn’t consented or has withdrawn consent — unless processing that data is genuinely essential to delivering the service. Second, data collection must stay limited to what’s absolutely required for the intended purpose; only the minimal amount needed may be gathered.
tips.caveats: The deciding factor is simple: is this data truly essential to providing the service? Location data is essential for a map app, but contact lists aren’t needed for a flashlight app. After installing an app, head to your phone’s settings under app permissions and turn off any nonessential permissions. Grant access only when you genuinely need them, and even then, limit it to a one-time permission.

tips.title: You have the right to view, copy, correct, and delete your personal information; if refused, you can sue.
tips.cost: There is no cost involved. Only if the company drags its feet do you need to file a complaint or sue. A lawsuit typically takes several months to resolve, and you must pay legal fees yourself. Therefore, filing a complaint first is the more cost-effective option. The difficult part is having to repeatedly follow up when the company delays action.
tips.inPlainWords: You have the right to demand that a company let you view, copy, correct, and delete your personal information. When a service is discontinued, its retention period expires, or you withdraw consent, the company is obligated to delete that data on its own. If it refuses your request, it must provide a valid reason; otherwise, you can take it to court. Deactivating an account and deleting personal information are two separate actions — after deactivating, you must separately request deletion.
tips.benefit: There are several situations in which a company must proactively delete personal information: when a service is discontinued, when the agreed retention period ends, when you withdraw consent, or when the original purpose of data collection has been fulfilled. If it fails to do so, you can demand deletion. Should it deny your rights without justification, you may file a lawsuit.
tips.caveats: Deactivating an account and deleting personal information are distinct processes; after deactivating, you must separately request deletion. Before switching phones or selling an old device, make sure to log out of all accounts, unlink them, and then perform a factory reset. The law grants you a right to deletion after the fact — it cannot retrieve data that has already been leaked.

tips.title: You’re not required to use facial recognition: if other options exist, they must offer you alternatives if you refuse
tips.cost: No cost involved. When asked to use facial recognition, simply ask, “Are there any other verification methods available?” If they claim none exist, demand they provide alternatives. The challenge lies in actually voicing this question on the spot.
tips.inPlainWords: As long as any other method can achieve the same result, a service provider cannot force you to use facial recognition. If you decline facial recognition, they must offer alternatives such as a card swipe, password entry, or ID verification. They also cannot threaten that “the service won’t be provided” if you refuse. Installing facial recognition devices in hotel rooms, public showers, changing rooms, or restrooms is strictly prohibited.
tips.benefit: The Administrative Measures for the Safe Use of Facial Recognition Technology clearly state: “Where other non-facial recognition technologies can achieve the same purpose or meet equivalent operational requirements, facial recognition must not be used as the sole verification method. If an individual declines facial recognition for identity verification, other reasonable and convenient alternatives must be provided.” The measures further stipulate: “No organization or individual may mislead, deceive, or coerce individuals into accepting facial recognition for identity verification under the pretext of service delivery or improved quality.” Consent to use facial recognition must be “freely, explicitly, and separately given after full disclosure” — meaning you must be asked specifically about this and must agree independently. You retain the right to withdraw consent, and service providers must offer an easy way to do so. For minors under 14, parental or guardian consent is mandatory. In public spaces, facial recognition devices may only be installed if “necessary for public safety” and must display prominent warning signs. Their use inside private areas such as hotel rooms, showers, changing rooms, or restrooms is forbidden. Facial data must be stored locally on devices and must not be transmitted over the internet, except where permitted by law or with explicit consent (effective nationwide as of June 1, 2025).
tips.caveats: Common scenarios include residential building access systems, rental platforms, gyms, and hotels requesting facial data. When they claim “the system only supports facial recognition,” quote the exact wording from the regulations: “Where other non-facial recognition technologies can achieve the same purpose or meet equivalent operational requirements, facial recognition must not be used as the sole verification method.” Then demand alternative verification methods such as card swipes, passwords, or ID checks. If they still refuse, report them to local internet regulatory authorities. Certain financial and government services may have separate rules — follow those instead. Unlike passwords, facial data cannot be changed after a breach, so it demands greater caution. Organizations storing facial data on behalf of 100,000+ individuals must register with provincial or higher-level internet regulators within 30 days; this registration status can help you assess their legitimacy. Your rights to access, correct, or delete your personal data are covered in item 8.

tips.title: Do not entrust proprietary code, API keys, or confidential data to unverified "AI relay proxy stations," especially when allowing AI agents to execute local commands autonomously
tips.cost: Direct official API access is typically more expensive than third-party relay proxies, and recharging balances can be less convenient. The friction lies in the temptation: relay proxies are cheap and provide access to multiple foundational models through a single endpoint.
tips.inPlainWords: An intermediary proxy sits directly between you and the model provider: it can observe, intercept, and modify everything you send and receive. In an empirical study evaluating over 400 proxy stations, 9 injected malicious code into model responses, and 17 actively hijacked intentionally seeded cloud service credentials. If you allow AI agents to execute commands locally on your machine, a single tampered command is enough to compromise full system control.
tips.benefit: In June 2026, the Ministry of State Security issued a cybersecurity advisory warning that unverified third-party proxy relays retain submitted user data on remote servers, intercept proprietary code, or resell private datasets to other model providers for training. Some proxies conceal backdoors, injecting malicious payloads into user devices to harvest credentials and install remote administration trojans. The advisory strongly recommends using direct official API connections or officially licensed platforms while avoiding unlicensed, unverified proxies. Sensitive data and project documentation should be sanitized and desensitized before transmission, and API keys must be rotated regularly. If abnormal billing, unexplained bans, or data anomalies occur, discontinue service immediately, revoke keys, scan for malware, and preserve evidence. A 2026 empirical study by researchers at UC Santa Barbara and collaborator institutions evaluated 28 commercial relay services purchased across online storefronts and 400 public free proxies. Results showed that 1 paid service and 8 free proxies injected malicious code into returned tool-call outputs (system commands instructed by the AI to run on local machines, such as package installations). Furthermore, 2 services strategically timed their attacks, selectively targeting fully autonomous agent execution sessions. Seventeen proxies actively abused intentionally placed Amazon Web Services (AWS) credentials, and 1 drained test funds from an Ethereum test wallet (loss under $50). The study demonstrated subtle, stealthy tampering techniques: for instance, replacing standard packages like `requests` with typosquatted dependencies like `reqeusts` in command payloads, which easily escapes visual inspection.
tips.sources: Liu H, Shou C, Wen H, Chen Y, Fang RJ, Feng Y. (2026). Your Agent Is Mine: Measuring Malicious Intermediary Attacks on the LLM Supply Chain. arXiv:2604.08407. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08407>
tips.caveats: Rated Grade B because it relies on a single empirical preprint prior to peer-reviewed publication. The majority of evaluated relays were free public endpoints, with only 28 commercial services tested, precluding an exact statistical percentage of compromised market share. Some media reports mistakenly exaggerated the test wallet theft to $500,000; the actual loss reported in the paper was under $50. Benefit is rated medium due to the severity of credential leaks and device takeover risks, though individual financial losses vary. If you have previously routed sensitive requests through unknown proxies, immediately revoke and regenerate affected API keys with the official model provider, as well as any exposed cloud provider and code repository access tokens. When routing through third-party proxies, never grant AI agents unreviewed autonomous command execution—manually inspect every shell command before confirmation. For criminal liabilities associated with operating unauthorized proxy relays, see Chapter 11, Rule 19.

tips.title: Audit the SIM cards and bank accounts linked to your identity once a year
tips.cost: No cost. The TAFCOP check is free, and the annual credit report is free.
tips.inPlainWords: India limits the number of SIM cards a person may hold. Use the Sanchar Saathi or TAFCOP portal to see the mobile connections in your name and report an unknown one. Check your credit report for a loan or card you did not apply for, and close an unused account. An unknown SIM can be used for OTP fraud.
tips.benefit: The Department of Telecommunications' TAFCOP lets you check the mobile connections issued against your ID and report the unauthorised ones. The RBI's KYC rules require the bank to verify the customer. A credit bureau report shows a loan or card in your name. The Aadhaar Act restricts the use of Aadhaar. The BNS and the IT Act cover identity theft.
tips.sources: Department of Telecommunications, Sanchar Saathi. <https://sancharsaathi.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, KYC. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; TransUnion CIBIL. <https://www.cibil.com/>; Aadhaar Act, 2016. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: A family member may have used your ID for a SIM; ask before reporting. A closed account can still show for a month. Do not share an OTP with anyone who offers to 'check' your SIM.

tips.title: Before canceling or changing a mobile phone number, migrate or unbind all linked online services and update your bank registration
tips.cost: Zero financial outlay. Requires migrating accounts individually to your new number, and updating bank-registered mobile numbers via banking apps or physical branches. Accounts with extensive bindings take 1 to 2 hours. The difficulty is remembering rarely used legacy services.
tips.inPlainWords: Once a mobile phone number is cancelled, telecommunications carriers are legally permitted to reissue that recycled number to a new subscriber after just 90 days. If your old accounts remain linked to that number, SMS two-factor verification codes will route directly to the new subscriber's handset, potentially allowing them to log into your accounts. Always migrate critical payment apps, digital wallets, and bank records before disconnecting your number.
tips.benefit: National Telecommunications Service Specifications mandate that the minimum quarantine freeze period for mobile phone numbers is 90 days (measured from cancellation to reissue), after which numbers may be reassigned to the public pool. MIIT's Q1 2025 Telecommunications Service Quality Bulletin highlighted the carrier "Recycled Number Renewal" feature within operator apps, enabling new subscribers to unbind accounts registered by previous owners prior to line activation. The Q2 2026 bulletin noted that this service covered 258 mainstream internet applications with over 850 million unbinding requests processed. The necessity of new subscribers having to unbind past accounts confirms that legacy accounts frequently remain bound to recycled numbers. In 2024 interviews with People's Posts and Telecom, carrier customer service representatives confirmed that new number owners can log into legacy accounts via SMS verification codes if previous holders failed to unbind them, strongly advising subscribers to unlink WeChat, Alipay, and bank registration numbers prior to number cancellation.
tips.sources: Ministry of Information Industry (2005). Telecommunications Service Specifications (MII Order No. 36, Appendix 2, Item 2.1.7). <https://www.miit.gov.cn/zwgk/zcwj/flfg/art/2020/art_0cff75e226764dc7b811cd4e954415c5.html>; Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (2025). Bulletin on Telecommunications Service Quality for Q1 2025 (MIIT Letter [2025] No. 85). <https://www.miit.gov.cn/jgsj/xgj/fwjd/art/2025/art_1bcadc32bf8141a8b616db8eaadba2e9.html>; Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (2026). Bulletin on Telecommunications Service Quality for Q2 2026 (MIIT Letter [2026] No. 258). <https://nmca.miit.gov.cn/xwdt/xydt/art/2026/art_2f6af9120a064a6784557cdefbf1c5be.html>; Li Yue (2024). Three Major Carriers Remind Users: Unbind Accounts Before Changing or Canceling Numbers. People's Posts and Telecom / Tibet CAC. <https://wxb.xzdw.gov.cn/wlaq/aqdt/202404/t20240408_456634.html> (Archive: <https://web.archive.org/web/20250414055537/https://wxb.xzdw.gov.cn/wlaq/aqdt/202404/t20240408_456634.html>)
tips.caveats: First use "One ID All Queries 2.0" to audit how many platforms are tied to your old number (see Chapter 14, Rule 11). Update high-risk financial and payment accounts first, then social platforms, and delete unused legacy accounts. After migrating accounts, maintain the old number on a minimal maintenance plan for 1 to 2 months to catch any overlooked SMS verification prompts. Managing unauthorized device logins is covered in Chapter 14, Rule 6. Sanitizing old phones and performing factory resets prior to sale is addressed in Chapter 14, Rule 8 notes. Graded Evidence Grade C due to qualitative operational advisories from carriers and regulators. Benefit is categorized as Moderate. Beneficiary is yourself.
